11 — Pixels and Language

“Look at the green ball”: a head camera, a colour, a turn, and a check · SOC4180 Robot and AI

Hong Jeong

“Look at the green ball”

The G1 stands in front of four coloured balls with a camera in its head. It is told, in words, which one to look at. This week’s one file, lab.py, does it in four steps:

  1. Words → a colour. Pick the colour out of the sentence; refuse a word it does not know.
  2. Pixels → a direction. Find that colour in the camera picture (find_ball, the function you change).
  3. A turn. Turn the waist until the ball sits in the middle of the picture (a P controller, week 5).
  4. A check. Look again and confirm, with the picture; refuse if the ball is not there.

Steps 1 and 2 have famous learned versions (a convolutional network, a vision-language model); we meet them on two slides with their measured numbers. The week’s point is step 4: a robot that acts on what it believes must check, and a check made with the same sense that was wrong passes its own mistake.

Layer: the camera is a Layer 2 sensor; reading it, and the words, are Layer 5.

Where this week sits on the map

Week 8 opened with a map of RL methods (value- or policy-based, model-based or free, on- or off-policy, table or function). The course’s route through it:

week method what is learned the step from the week before
7 value iteration \(V^*\), \(\pi^*\) on a grid exact, but needs \(P\) and \(R\) as tables
7b Q-learning, SARSA a \(Q\) table drops \(P\): learns from samples
8 policy gradient, parameter-space search one ankle gain \(\theta\) drops the table: a policy with a parameter
9 PPO + domain randomisation two networks (shipped) scales \(\theta\) to a network; trains in many worlds
10 MPPI; behaviour cloning a plan every step; a copy uses the simulator as a model; learns from an expert, not a reward
11 (this week) perception and a check — the policy’s input becomes pixels and words

The policy’s input changes: from a tilt to pixels and words. Their learned versions (a CNN, a vision–language model) are trained like week 9’s networks; this week’s point is the check that any learned policy needs.

\({\color{#3b7dd8}{a,\ e}}\); \({\color{#3b7dd8}{X,\ Y,\ Z}}\) a direction (azimuth, left +; elevation, up +); a point in the camera’s frame (right, up, forward) blue

Four questions, in order: how does a point land on a pixel, how do you find a colour in a picture, what happens when the robot turns on it, and how does it know it worked.

The camera: a body-fixed frame

spec = mujoco.MjSpec.from_file(str(soc4180.robot_path()))       # inside soc4180.vision.camera_model
spec.body("torso_link").add_camera(name="head", pos=[0.08, 0, 0.45],
                                   xyaxes=[0, -1, 0, 0, 0, 1], fovy=90)
ball = spec.worldbody.add_body(name="ball_green", mocap=True, pos=[1.2, 0, 0.8])
ball.add_geom(type=mujoco.mjtGeom.mjGEOM_SPHERE, size=[0.15, 0, 0],
              rgba=[0.1, 0.8, 0.1, 1], contype=0, conaffinity=0)
  • A camera hangs on a body, like a site: it moves with the torso. The G1 has no neck, so the waist is the only way to aim it.
  • MuJoCo cameras look down their own −z. xyaxes names the camera’s x (picture right) and y (picture up) in the body frame: right = torso −y, up = +z, so it looks along +x, forward.
  • fovy = 90: the picture spans 90° top to bottom, so its edge is 45° from the middle. The picture is square, so the same holds across.
  • contype = conaffinity = 0: nothing can touch a ball. It is a target, not an object.

    def step(self, seconds: float):
        """Run the physics with the current ``ctrl``, keeping the balls where they are."""
        d = self.data
        for _ in range(int(round(seconds / self.model.opt.timestep))):
            d.mocap_pos[:] = self.balls
            mujoco.mj_step(self.model, d)
            if round(d.time / self.model.opt.timestep) % 17 == 0:
                self.frames.append(d.qpos.copy())

Body lives in soc4180.agent. lab.py never calls mujoco.mj_step itself: it sets a servo target in body.data.ctrl and asks the body to run.

def scene(body, seed, hide=None):
    """Balls at random directions (seeded); `hide` puts one behind the robot."""
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    az = rng.permutation(np.linspace(-0.7, 0.7, 4)) + rng.uniform(-0.1, 0.1, 4)
    balls = {n: (float(a), float(rng.uniform(-0.2, 0.15)), float(rng.uniform(1.4, 2.2)))
             for n, a in zip(("red", "green", "blue", "yellow"), az)}
    if hide:
        balls[hide] = (math.pi, 0.0, 2.0)
    body.reset(balls)

scene 2: red +43.7 deg   green  +8.7 deg   blue -39.0 deg   yellow -10.7 deg

What the robot sees

The lab works on the left picture: 64 × 64 pixels is enough to find a ball by its colour. The white lines mark the middle, where the robot wants the named ball to be.

From a direction to a pixel

Step 1: similar triangles. A pinhole camera with its picture at distance \({\color{#e8743b}{f}}\) puts a point (\({\color{#3b7dd8}{X}}, {\color{#3b7dd8}{Y}}, {\color{#3b7dd8}{Z}}\)) (right, up, forward) at \({\color{#e8743b}{f}}{\color{#3b7dd8}{X}}/{\color{#3b7dd8}{Z}}\) across and \({\color{#e8743b}{f}}{\color{#3b7dd8}{Y}}/{\color{#3b7dd8}{Z}}\) up. A camera divides by depth: twice as far in the same direction is the same pixel.

Step 2: the direction as a point. A ball at distance \(D\), azimuth \({\color{#3b7dd8}{a}}\) (left +), elevation \({\color{#3b7dd8}{e}}\) (up +): \[{\color{#3b7dd8}{X}} = -D\cos{\color{#3b7dd8}{e}}\sin{\color{#3b7dd8}{a}},\quad {\color{#3b7dd8}{Y}} = D\sin{\color{#3b7dd8}{e}},\quad {\color{#3b7dd8}{Z}} = D\cos{\color{#3b7dd8}{e}}\cos{\color{#3b7dd8}{a}}\] (the minus: azimuth counts to the left, the picture’s x points right).

Step 3: divide by depth, with \({\color{#e8743b}{f}} = 1\) and \({\color{#e8743b}{v}}\) counting down; \(D\) cancels: \[{\color{#e8743b}{u}} = \frac{{\color{#3b7dd8}{X}}}{{\color{#3b7dd8}{Z}}} = -\tan{\color{#3b7dd8}{a}}, \qquad {\color{#e8743b}{v}} = -\frac{{\color{#3b7dd8}{Y}}}{{\color{#3b7dd8}{Z}}} = -\frac{\tan{\color{#3b7dd8}{e}}}{\cos{\color{#3b7dd8}{a}}} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad {\color{#3b7dd8}{a}} = \arctan(-{\color{#e8743b}{u}})\]

The \(\cos{\color{#3b7dd8}{e}}\) cancels in \({\color{#e8743b}{u}}\): the column depends on the azimuth alone, whatever the height. So turning needs only \({\color{#e8743b}{u}}\), and lab.py computes azimuth = math.atan(-u). With a 90° view the edge is \(\tan 45° = 1\), so \({\color{#e8743b}{u}} \in [-1, 1]\) fills the picture.

Checking the formula against the simulator

img = picture
for i, name in enumerate(COLOURS):
    u, v = lab.find_ball(img, COLOURS[name])                        # the lab's detector (next slides)
    seen = math.degrees(math.atan(-u))                              # pixel -> azimuth, as in lab.obey
    true = math.degrees(ball_direction(body.model, body.data, i)[0])  # from the simulator's ball position
    print(f"{name:6s}  u = {u:+.3f}   atan(-u) = {seen:+6.1f} deg   simulator: {true:+6.1f} deg   "
          f"difference {seen - true:+.1f}")
print(f"10 degrees is {32 * math.tan(math.radians(10)):.1f} pixels near the middle, "
      f"{32 * (1 - math.tan(math.radians(35))):.1f} between 35 and 45 degrees")
red     u = +0.969   atan(-u) =  -44.1 deg   simulator:  -44.2 deg   difference +0.1
green   u = +0.151   atan(-u) =   -8.6 deg   simulator:   -8.2 deg   difference -0.4
blue    u = -0.203   atan(-u) =  +11.5 deg   simulator:  +11.2 deg   difference +0.3
yellow  u = -0.863   atan(-u) =  +40.8 deg   simulator:  +39.2 deg   difference +1.6
10 degrees is 5.6 pixels near the middle, 9.6 between 35 and 45 degrees

ball_direction reads the ball’s true position out of the simulator; the robot never sees it. The picture agrees with it to within 1.5°, from a 64-pixel picture and one line of trigonometry. And because of the \(\tan\), pixels are not evenly spaced in angle: the same 10° covers fewer pixels near the middle than near the edge.

A picture is numbers

print(f"picture: shape {img.shape}, dtype {img.dtype}, {img.size:,} numbers from {img.min()} to {img.max()}")

col, row = int((u + 1) / 2 * img.shape[1]), int((v + 1) / 2 * img.shape[0])
for label, (rr, cc) in (("at the green ball", (row, col)), ("top-left corner", (0, 0)), ("bottom row", (63, 32))):
    p = img[rr, cc] / 255.0
    d = np.linalg.norm(p - np.asarray(COLOURS["green"]))
    print(f"pixel (row {rr:2d}, col {cc:2d}) {label:18s} RGB {np.round(p, 2)}   distance to green {d:.2f}")
print("green ball's colour in the model:", COLOURS["green"])
picture: shape (64, 64, 3), dtype uint8, 12,288 numbers from 3 to 246
pixel (row 30, col 36) at the green ball  RGB [0.11 0.78 0.11]   distance to green 0.03
pixel (row  0, col  0) top-left corner    RGB [0.23 0.38 0.53]   distance to green 0.62
pixel (row 63, col 32) bottom row         RGB [0.15 0.23 0.31]   distance to green 0.61
green ball's colour in the model: (0.1, 0.8, 0.1)

Each pixel is three numbers (red, green, blue), stored as uint8, 0 to 255; divided by 255 they are a point \({\color{#2a9d5c}{\mathbf{p}}}\) in the unit cube. The ball is drawn with colour \({\color{#2a9d5c}{\mathbf{c}}}\), but its pixels are not exactly \({\color{#2a9d5c}{\mathbf{c}}}\): lighting shades the sphere. So “find green” cannot mean “find pixels equal to green”. It has to mean close to green.

The simplest detector

Close to the colour. For every pixel, the straight-line distance in RGB: \[{\color{#c0392b}{d}}_{ij} = \lVert {\color{#2a9d5c}{\mathbf{p}}}_{ij} - {\color{#2a9d5c}{\mathbf{c}}} \rVert = \sqrt{(r_{ij} - c_r)^2 + (g_{ij} - c_g)^2 + (b_{ij} - c_b)^2}, \qquad 0 \le {\color{#c0392b}{d}} \le \sqrt 3 \approx 1.73\] A pixel counts if \({\color{#c0392b}{d}}_{ij} < {\color{#c0392b}{\tau}}\) (THRESHOLD, 0.25 as shipped). Call the set of counted pixels \(S\), with \(|S|\) members.

Not there. If \(|S| <\) MIN_PIXELS (4), answer none. This is the detector saying “I do not see it”, and the lab’s refusal depends on it.

Where. The centre of the counted pixels (their mean row and column), as picture coordinates, a pixel’s centre at \(+0.5\): \[{\color{#e8743b}{u}} = \frac{\overline{\text{col}} + 0.5}{W}\cdot 2 - 1, \qquad {\color{#e8743b}{v}} = \frac{\overline{\text{row}} + 0.5}{H}\cdot 2 - 1\]

No learning and no model of a ball: a colour, a distance, a count, a mean. Every number it uses is one you can print, which is why it is the one you change.

find_ball, from lab.py

print(f"THRESHOLD = {lab.THRESHOLD}      MIN_PIXELS = {lab.MIN_PIXELS}\n")
print(inspect.getsource(lab.find_ball))
THRESHOLD = 0.25      MIN_PIXELS = 4

def find_ball(image, rgb):
    pixels = image.astype(float) / 255.0
    distance = np.linalg.norm(pixels - np.asarray(rgb), axis=-1)       # (H, W)
    rows, cols = np.nonzero(distance < THRESHOLD)
    if len(rows) < MIN_PIXELS:
        return None
    h, w = distance.shape
    u = (cols.mean() + 0.5) / w * 2 - 1
    v = (rows.mean() + 0.5) / h * 2 - 1
    return u, v

Each line is one line of the last slide: scale to \(0..1\), the distance image (H, W), np.nonzero for the set \(S\), the count test, the two means. image is the (64, 64, 3) picture; rgb is the colour from step 1. It returns (u, v) or None.

find_ball, line by line: the distance

code what it does why
image.astype(float) / 255.0 uint8 0..255 → floats 0..1, still (64, 64, 3) the same scale as rgb: COLOURS are 0..1
np.asarray(rgb) the ball’s colour \({\color{#2a9d5c}{\mathbf{c}}}\) as an array of 3 a tuple cannot be subtracted from an array
pixels - np.asarray(rgb) NumPy broadcasts (64, 64, 3) minus (3,): \({\color{#2a9d5c}{\mathbf{p}}}_{ij} - {\color{#2a9d5c}{\mathbf{c}}}\) for every pixel 4,096 subtractions, no loop
np.linalg.norm(..., axis=-1) the length along the last axis (r, g, b), so distance is (H, W) \({\color{#c0392b}{d}}_{ij}\), one number per pixel
# (0..1.7) (the comment on THRESHOLD) 0 is the exact colour; the most is opposite corners of the colour cube, black to white, \(\sqrt 3 \approx 1.73\) the scale \({\color{#c0392b}{\tau}}\) = 0.25 is read on 
print("black to white:", np.linalg.norm(np.array([1.0, 1.0, 1.0]) - np.array([0.0, 0.0, 0.0])))
black to white: 1.7320508075688772

find_ball, line by line: where

code what it does why
distance < THRESHOLD True where \({\color{#c0392b}{d}} < {\color{#c0392b}{\tau}}\): a (64, 64) mask the set \(S\)
rows, cols = np.nonzero(...) the row and the column of every True, two arrays of length \(\lvert S\rvert\) the positions of the counted pixels
if len(rows) < MIN_PIXELS: return None fewer than 4 counted pixels → None “not there”: obey turns it into a refusal
cols.mean(), rows.mean() the centroid: the mean column and row (may be a fraction) the blob’s centre is the ball’s direction

find_ball, line by line: where (cont.)

code what it does why
+ 0.5 pixel c covers c to c + 1; its centre is c + 0.5 without it every answer is half a pixel off, and the middle would not be 0
/ w * 2 - 1 (h, w = distance.shape) 0 .. w → \({\color{#e8743b}{u}}\) in -1 .. +1; the same for \({\color{#e8743b}{v}}\) with h the \({\color{#e8743b}{u}}\) of From a direction to a pixel: \(\tan 45° = 1\) at the edge
return u, v obey uses only u the column alone gives the azimuth

What find_ball sees

At \({\color{#c0392b}{\tau}} = 0.25\) each colour picks out one blob and nothing else, and the centre of the blob is the ball’s direction: the floor and the sky are farther than 0.25 from every ball colour. The blobs are small, and red, at the edge of the picture, gives exactly 4 pixels: MIN_PIXELS is 4, so it is seen by the narrowest possible margin.

The threshold decides what “green” means

def counted(image, rgb, tau):
    return int((np.linalg.norm(image / 255.0 - np.asarray(rgb), axis=-1) < tau).sum())
print(f"{'tau':>5} " + " ".join(f"{n:>7}" for n in COLOURS))
for tau in (0.05, 0.25, 0.6):
    print(f"{tau:5.2f} " + " ".join(f"{counted(img, COLOURS[n], tau):7d}" for n in COLOURS))
lab.scene(body, 1, hide="green")                                    # the green ball moved behind the robot
with _new_renderer(body.model, lab.RESOLUTION, lab.RESOLUTION) as r:
    r.update_scene(body.data, camera=CAMERA); no_green = r.render().copy()
for tau in (0.25, 0.6):
    print(f"green ball hidden, tau {tau}: {counted(no_green, COLOURS['green'], tau)} 'green' pixels")
lab.scene(body, 1)
  tau     red   green    blue  yellow
 0.05       0       4       1       2
 0.25       4      15      10       9
 0.60      44     497    2347      25
green ball hidden, tau 0.25: 0 'green' pixels
green ball hidden, tau 0.6: 462 'green' pixels

Too strict (0.05) and shading pushes almost every ball pixel out: fewer than MIN_PIXELS count. Too loose (0.6) and “green” swallows pixels that are not the green ball (the background sits only about 0.6 from green, last slide; “blue” takes half the picture), and there are “green” pixels even when the green ball is behind the robot. The detector has no idea it is wrong; it reports a centre either way.

Closing the loop

Ten times a second (body.step(0.1)): find the ball, read its azimuth, move the waist’s target: \[\text{waist}_{k+1} = \text{waist}_k + {\color{#8e44ad}{g}}\,{\color{#3b7dd8}{a_k}}, \qquad {\color{#3b7dd8}{a_k}} = \arctan(-{\color{#e8743b}{u_k}})\]

A model of the loop. The ball sits at bearing \({\color{#3b7dd8}{\beta}}\); the camera points at heading \({\color{#3b7dd8}{\psi_k}}\); the azimuth in the picture is the error \({\color{#3b7dd8}{a_k}} = {\color{#3b7dd8}{\beta}} - {\color{#3b7dd8}{\psi_k}}\). If the waist reaches each target before the next picture, \({\color{#3b7dd8}{\psi_{k+1}}} = {\color{#3b7dd8}{\psi_k}} + {\color{#8e44ad}{g}}{\color{#3b7dd8}{a_k}}\). Subtract both sides from \({\color{#3b7dd8}{\beta}}\): \[{\color{#3b7dd8}{a_{k+1}}} = (1 - {\color{#8e44ad}{g}})\,{\color{#3b7dd8}{a_k}} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad {\color{#3b7dd8}{a_k}} = (1 - {\color{#8e44ad}{g}})^k\,{\color{#3b7dd8}{a_0}}\]

Closing the loop: what the gain does

gain \({\color{#8e44ad}{g}}\) \(1 - {\color{#8e44ad}{g}}\) the error, from 30° behaviour
0.3 +0.7 30 → 21 → 14.7 → 10.3 slow, no overshoot
0.8 (GAIN) +0.2 30 → 6 → 1.2 → 0.24 fast, no overshoot
1.5 −0.5 30 → −15 → +7.5 → −3.8 overshoots, decays
2.5 −1.5 30 → −45 → +67 → … flips and grows: unstable

It converges if and only if \(0 < {\color{#8e44ad}{g}} < 2\), and never overshoots for \({\color{#8e44ad}{g}} \le 1\). Week 5’s P controller, now with a camera as the sensor (visual servoing).

Four gains on the robot

red   gain 0.3: done: red in the middle (waist -44 deg)  standing True  furthest past the middle  -0.0 deg
red   gain 0.8: done: red in the middle (waist -46 deg)  standing True  furthest past the middle  +8.4 deg
red   gain 1.5: refused: I do not see a red ball         standing False furthest past the middle +22.7 deg
red   gain 2.5: refused: I do not see a red ball         standing False furthest past the middle +31.7 deg
green gain 0.3: done: green in the middle (waist -8 deg) standing True  furthest past the middle  +0.4 deg
green gain 0.8: done: green in the middle (waist -8 deg) standing True  furthest past the middle  +0.4 deg
green gain 1.5: done: green in the middle (waist -8 deg) standing True  furthest past the middle  +2.7 deg
green gain 2.5: done: green in the middle (waist -4 deg) standing True  furthest past the middle  +7.7 deg

Red starts 44° off, at the edge of the picture. 0.3 creeps in; 0.8 overshoots by 8°, which the model says cannot happen below 1; at 1.5 and 2.5 the torso swings back and forth, the robot starts to fall (standing False), the ball leaves the picture and the robot refuses. Green starts 8° off and every gain, even 2.5, settles: the model says 2.5 must diverge, but the waist twists the pelvis the other way and the camera turns less than commanded (measured in an earlier version: a 28° command turned the camera 66 % of it in 0.1 s). The body is not the model, and a large error is where that matters.

Words → a colour

print(inspect.getsource(lab.colour_of))
for words in ("look at the green ball", "LOOK AT THE GREEN BALL!", "the crimson one",
              "not the red one, the blue one", "greenish"):
    print(f"{words!r:34s} -> {lab.colour_of(words)}")
def colour_of(words):
    from soc4180.vision import COLOURS
    known = [w for w in re.findall(r"[a-z]+", words.lower()) if w in COLOURS]
    return known[0] if known else None

'look at the green ball'           -> green
'LOOK AT THE GREEN BALL!'          -> green
'the crimson one'                  -> None
'not the red one, the blue one'    -> red
'greenish'                         -> None

Lower-case, split into words, keep the ones that name a ball colour, take the first. That is a lookup table with four entries: it never guesses, which is its strength (“crimson” gets None, so the robot refuses). It is also its limit: “crimson” is red to a person, “greenish” is not a word it knows, and “not the red one” picks red, because a list of words has no grammar.

colour_of, line by line

code what it does why
from soc4180.vision import COLOURS the dictionary of ball colours its four keys, red green blue yellow, are the only words the robot knows
words.lower() "LOOK AT THE GREEN BALL!" → "look at the green ball!" the pattern below matches lower case only
re.findall(r"[a-z]+", ...) every run of letters: ["look", "at", "the", "green", "ball"] spaces and punctuation split words; "greenish" stays one word
if w in COLOURS keeps a word only if it is exactly a key "crimson" and "greenish" are dropped
known[0] the first colour word "not the red one, the blue one" → red
else None no colour word at all obey refuses at once, before anything moves

A list comprehension ([w for w in ... if ...]) is a loop and a filter in one line.

obey: one instruction, from lab.py (1 of 2)

src = inspect.getsource(lab.obey).splitlines()
print("\n".join(src[:20]))
def obey(body, renderer, words, dim=1.0):
    from soc4180.vision import CAMERA, COLOURS, ball_direction

    colour = colour_of(words)
    if colour is None:
        return False, "refused: no colour I know in those words", None
    rgb = np.asarray(COLOURS[colour]) * dim
    w = body.act("waist_yaw")
    lo, hi = body.model.actuator_ctrlrange[w]

    def picture():
        renderer.update_scene(body.data, camera=CAMERA)
        return renderer.render()

    for _ in range(20):                                            # 2 s of looking and turning
        uv = find_ball(picture(), rgb)
        if uv is None:
            return False, f"refused: I do not see a {colour} ball", None
        azimuth = math.atan(-uv[0])
        body.data.ctrl[w] = float(np.clip(body.data.ctrl[w] + GAIN * azimuth, lo, hi))

Step 1 refuses before anything moves. rgb * dim is the colour to look for (the --dim experiment scales the lights and tells the robot so). The loop is the last two slides: 20 pictures, 2 s; inside it, a None from find_ball is an immediate refusal.

obey, line by line: before the loop

code what it does why
from soc4180.vision import CAMERA, COLOURS, ball_direction the camera’s name "head", the colours, and the simulator’s answer key ball_direction is used only for the reported truth
colour = colour_of(words); if colour is None: return False, ..., None step 1, and a refusal before anything moves None as the third value prints as -
rgb = np.asarray(COLOURS[colour]) * dim the colour to look for, every channel scaled by dim (30 % at --dim 0.3) dimmer lights make darker pixels; the robot is told the light level
w = body.act("waist_yaw") the waist-yaw servo’s actuator index body.data.ctrl[w] is the waist’s target angle

(continued on the next slide)

obey, line by line: before the loop (cont.)

code what it does why
lo, hi = body.model.actuator_ctrlrange[w] the target’s limits, −2.618 .. +2.618 rad (the joint’s range) the loop must never ask for an angle the joint cannot reach
renderer.update_scene(body.data, camera=CAMERA) copies the robot’s and the balls’ current poses into the renderer, seen from head a picture of now, after the last turn
renderer.render() draws and returns a (64, 64, 3) uint8 array the image that find_ball reads

picture() is defined inside obey, so it can use body and renderer without being passed them. The renderer was made once, in main, at RESOLUTION.

obey, line by line: the loop

code what it does why
for _ in range(20): 20 rounds of 0.1 s 2 s of looking and turning
uv = find_ball(picture(), rgb) a new picture, then the ball in it the sensor read, every round
if uv is None: return False, f"refused: ...", None the ball left the picture (gain 2.5) or was never in it (hidden) refuse at once, and say why
azimuth = math.atan(-uv[0]) \({\color{#3b7dd8}{a}} = \arctan(-{\color{#e8743b}{u}})\), radians, left + only \({\color{#e8743b}{u}}\): the column depends on the azimuth alone
body.data.ctrl[w] + GAIN * azimuth the new waist target: old target \(+\ {\color{#8e44ad}{g}}\,{\color{#3b7dd8}{a}}\) the P step of Closing the loop
np.clip(..., lo, hi), float(...) keeps the target in range; one plain number into ctrl a safe command
body.step(0.1) (first line of the next slide) 0.1 s of physics: the waist servo moves toward the target the next picture sees the turned body

The loop never stops early on success: it always runs 20 rounds, then checks.

obey: the check (2 of 2)

print("\n".join(src[20:]))
        body.step(0.1)

    uv = find_ball(picture(), rgb)                                 # the check, from the picture
    truth = math.degrees(ball_direction(body.model, body.data, ["red", "green", "blue", "yellow"].index(colour))[0])
    if not body.standing:
        return False, "failed: fell over while turning", truth
    if uv is None or abs(math.degrees(math.atan(-uv[0]))) > CENTRED_DEG:
        return False, f"failed: the {colour} ball is not in the middle", truth
    return True, f"done: {colour} in the middle (waist {math.degrees(body.data.qpos[body.act_q[w]]):+.0f} deg)", truth

After turning, one more picture, and the same detector must find the ball within CENTRED_DEG (5°) of the middle, with the robot still standing. truth comes from the simulator and is only reported, as the “true error” column: the robot’s own answer never uses it. On a real robot that column does not exist.

obey, line by line: the check and the true error

code what it does why
uv = find_ball(picture(), rgb) one more picture after the 20th turn the check, made with the same detector
["red", "green", "blue", "yellow"].index(colour) the ball’s mocap index, in the order Body made them which ball to ask the simulator about
ball_direction(body.model, body.data, i)[0] the ball’s true azimuth from the camera, from mocap_pos and the camera’s pose; [0] azimuth, [1] elevation the answer key; math.degrees for the table
if not body.standing: the pelvis dropped below 0.6 m or tilted over 20° “failed: fell over while turning”

(continued on the next slide)

obey, line by line: the check and the true error (cont.)

code what it does why
uv is None or abs(math.degrees(math.atan(-uv[0]))) > CENTRED_DEG not found, or more than 5° from the middle in the picture “failed: … not in the middle”
body.data.qpos[body.act_q[w]] the angle the waist actually reached reported in “done”, in degrees
return ..., truth truth is the third value of all three answers printed as “true error”

No if in obey reads truth. Every decision (refuse, fail, done) is made from the picture and body.standing. Set truth = None instead and the robot behaves identically; only the table loses its column.

    if args.no_viewer or soc4180.is_colab():
        return 0
    scene(body, 1)

                    break
                d.qpos[:] = q; mujoco.mj_forward(body.model, d); viewer.sync()
                time.sleep(17 * body.model.opt.timestep)

    return 0

The next slides run the same ten tests from the notebook, with one setting changed at a time.

The battery: lab.py’s ten tests, one setting changed

def battery(threshold=0.25, dim=1.0, gain=0.8, min_pixels=4, show=False):
    """lab.py's ten tests (8 looks, a hidden ball, an unknown word) with one setting changed."""
    keep = lab.THRESHOLD, lab.GAIN, lab.MIN_PIXELS
    lab.THRESHOLD, lab.GAIN, lab.MIN_PIXELS = threshold, gain, min_pixels
    b = Body()
    if dim != 1.0:                                                   # as lab.py --dim
        b.model.light_diffuse[:] *= dim; b.model.light_ambient[:] *= dim
    tests = [(s, None, f"look at the {c} ball") for s in (1, 2) for c in COLOURS]
    tests += [(1, "green", "look at the green ball"), (1, None, "look at the crimson ball")]
    rows = []
    with _new_renderer(b.model, lab.RESOLUTION, lab.RESOLUTION) as rend:
        for seed, hide, words in tests:
            lab.scene(b, seed, hide); ok, msg, truth = lab.obey(b, rend, words, dim)
            rows.append((seed, hide, words, ok, msg, truth))
            if show:
                t = f"{truth:+6.1f} deg" if truth is not None else "-"
                print(f"{seed}{' no ' + hide if hide else '':9s} {words:25s} {msg:46s} {t:>10}")
    lab.THRESHOLD, lab.GAIN, lab.MIN_PIXELS = keep
    return rows

def summary(label, rows):
    looks = [r for r in rows if r[1] is None and "crimson" not in r[2]]
    done = [r for r in looks if r[3]]
    worst = max((abs(r[5]) for r in done), default=float("nan"))
    hid = next(r for r in rows if r[1])
    print(f"{label:16s} done {sum(r[3] for r in rows):2d} of 10 | looks done {len(done)} of 8, worst true error "
          f"{worst:5.1f} deg | hidden ball: {'DONE' if hid[3] else 'refused'}"
          + (f" ({hid[5]:+.0f} deg)" if hid[5] is not None else ""))

battery runs lab.py’s tests (8 looks, the green ball hidden, “crimson”); summary gives one line: looks “done”, their worst true error, the hidden ball. Setting lab.THRESHOLD works like editing the file: find_ball reads it when it runs.

Eight looks done within a fraction of a degree, the hidden ball refused, the unknown word refused. All ten answers are right; the same table is what lab.py prints on your laptop.

The learned versions

The lab hand-writes steps 1 and 2. Earlier versions of this week trained networks for both; measured then, with torch.set_num_threads(4) (not re-run here):

A small CNN reads the direction from pixels (3 convolutions + 2 linear layers, 146,370 parameters, 4,000 rendered red-ball pictures, labels free from the simulator):

trained on red ball, as trained blue ball dim room (30 %)
red balls only 1.0° 27.8° 15.2°
random colour and light (visual randomisation) 4.4° 9.4° 4.2°

Always guessing the average direction: 26.0°. The network is excellent on the world it was shown and worse than guessing on a ball of another colour; randomising the pictures fixes what it randomises, and costs accuracy on the easy case.

A words + pixels attention model (a bag of words → a query; the picture → a key per cell; the named ball’s cell by a softmax; 20,032 parameters): 2.0° on phrasings it was trained on, 2.1° on new phrasings, about 31° (chance) for “crimson”, the same as no colour word at all.

Confidently wrong

The same attention model, asked for a ball that is behind the robot: its heat map still peaked, mean 0.60 and up to 0.98, against a mean of 0.88 when the ball was there (200 pictures, measured as above). It had only ever been shown pictures with the ball present, so it had no way to say “not here”. The CNN, likewise, gives a direction for any picture at all.

can it say “I do not see it”? what it does on a world it was not shown
find_ball yes: fewer than MIN_PIXELS pixels depends on THRESHOLD (next slides)
the CNN no 27.8° off on a blue ball, no warning
the attention model no points at something, confidence up to 0.98

A network’s own output is not a check on that network. So a robot needs a check, and the check must not share the failure. The lab’s check uses the same find_ball. Watch what that buys.

The check that passes its own mistake

t0 = time.time()
summary("as shipped", shipped)
summary("THRESHOLD 0.05", battery(threshold=0.05))
summary("THRESHOLD 0.6", battery(threshold=0.6))
summary("--dim 0.3", battery(dim=0.3))
g25 = battery(gain=2.5); summary("GAIN 2.5", g25)
print("  GAIN 2.5 refuses:", "; ".join(f"scene {r[0]} {r[2].split()[3]} (shipped waist {s[4].split()[-2]} deg)"
                                     for r, s in zip(g25, shipped) if not r[3] and r[1] is None and "crimson" not in r[2]))
summary("MIN_PIXELS 1", battery(min_pixels=1))
print(f"({time.time() - t0:.0f} s)")
as shipped       done  8 of 10 | looks done 8 of 8, worst true error   0.8 deg | hidden ball: refused
THRESHOLD 0.05   done  0 of 10 | looks done 0 of 8, worst true error   nan deg | hidden ball: refused
THRESHOLD 0.6    done  9 of 10 | looks done 8 of 8, worst true error  39.9 deg | hidden ball: DONE (+157 deg)
--dim 0.3        done  9 of 10 | looks done 8 of 8, worst true error  44.7 deg | hidden ball: DONE (-173 deg)
GAIN 2.5         done  4 of 10 | looks done 4 of 8, worst true error   2.2 deg | hidden ball: refused
  GAIN 2.5 refuses: scene 1 red (shipped waist -46 deg); scene 1 yellow (shipped waist +42 deg); scene 2 red (shipped waist +45 deg); scene 2 blue (shipped waist -41 deg)
MIN_PIXELS 1     done  8 of 10 | looks done 8 of 8, worst true error   0.8 deg | hidden ball: refused
(94 s)

Read the “true error” column the robot never sees. At THRESHOLD 0.6 and in the dim room the robot reports “done” on looks up to 39° and 41° off, and “done” on the hidden ball, half a turn away. Too strict (0.05) fails safely: it refuses everything. Gain 2.5 fails safely too: it loses the balls that need a large turn, and says so.

Why the check failed, and what would catch it

The check asks the detector that made the mistake whether it made a mistake. At THRESHOLD 0.6 “green” includes pixels that are not the green ball, so find_ball centres on them, the robot turns to them, and the final picture shows them, centred. Same sense, same error, so the check agrees.

A check is worth something only if it can fail when the action failed: a second, independent sense.

The “true error” column is the one you may not use: it is the simulator’s answer key. On the term project, a claim of success needs a check that could have said no.

What would catch it

Candidates for the second sense, each with what it costs:

second sense catches still fooled by
the blob’s shape: a ball is a round blob of the right size for its distance a floor patch or a scatter of pixels counted as “green” a round green thing that is not the ball
a tighter threshold in the check than in the search loose matches that only pass the loose test dim light, which moves every pixel
another viewpoint: turn a little and predict where the ball must move in the picture a target that does not move like an object at that bearing nothing cheap
a different detector (a network) next to find_ball failures the two do not share failures they share (dim light hurts both)

Where a language model would fit

colour_of is the part a large language model replaces: given obey as a tool, it knows that crimson is red. It does not replace the check.

# Not run: it needs an API key, a network connection and the `anthropic` package (not in uv.lock).
import anthropic, lab
from soc4180.agent import Body
from soc4180.render import _new_renderer
client = anthropic.Anthropic()
look = {"name": "look", "description": "Turn the waist until the named ball is centred. Checks with the camera "
        "and says whether it worked.", "input_schema": {"type": "object", "required": ["colour"],
        "properties": {"colour": {"enum": ["red", "green", "blue", "yellow"]}}}}
body = Body(); rend = _new_renderer(body.model, lab.RESOLUTION, lab.RESOLUTION)
messages = [{"role": "user", "content": "Face the crimson ball."}]
while True:
    reply = client.messages.create(model="claude-opus-5-5", max_tokens=16000,
                                   tools=[look], messages=messages)
    messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": reply.content})
    if reply.stop_reason != "tool_use":
        break
    results = []
    for block in reply.content:
        if block.type == "tool_use":                     # run the skill; its check is the answer
            ok, msg, _ = lab.obey(body, rend, f"look at the {block.input['colour']} ball")
            results.append({"type": "tool_result", "tool_use_id": block.id, "content": msg, "is_error": not ok})
    messages.append({"role": "user", "content": results})          # all results in one message

A lookup fails loudly (None); a language model fails fluently, choosing a plausible colour for anything. The more general the planner, the more the check has to carry. Note what the tool returns: msg, the robot’s check, never the simulator’s truth.

Try (predict each first; what lab.py measured is in brackets):

  1. THRESHOLD = 0.05 or 0.6. [0.05 refuses all 10. 0.6 says “done” 9 times, up to 39° off, and “sees” the hidden green ball, 149° away.]

For your term project

Weeks 12–15 are the term project (projects README, catalogue). Projects that start here:

  • P11 — Eyes on the ball. Find a ball with the head camera and turn (or point) at it; which visual change breaks it: colour, light or distance?
  • P12 — Words to actions. A new word or a new skill for the robot, with a check that measures whether it worked, and refusals measured on scenes without the ball.
  • P4 — Reach while standing. Point a hand at the ball the camera found (IK, weeks 3-4).
  • P14 — Your own proposal, under the same method.

The method. (1) Predict first: write the number you expect and why. (2) A twin with one change: every claim is two runs differing in one setting (one threshold, one gain, one check). (3) results.csv: one row per run, every setting and every measured number, written by the script. (4) A CHECK line: the script prints whether the claim held (CHECK hidden ball refused: PASS). (5) Grade by margins: a pass line far from your number on both sides, and a measured wrong answer that fails.

Start from lab.py, soc4180.agent.Body and soc4180.vision (camera_model, place_ball, ball_direction, uv_of, angles_of_uv). The “true error” column is for grading your robot, never for your robot to use.
